title: Rare or Literary Structures

objectives: Understand and use: Advanced (formal/archaic) subjunctive — the bare base form of the verb (no -s, no "would/should") used after certain verbs/adjectives expressing necessity, demand, or recommendation, especially in formal American English and fixed expressions.

Understand and use: Emphatic "do" in literary contexts — "do/does/did" + bare infinitive used not to form a question or negative, but to add emphasis or formality, common in literary and rhetorical prose.

content.intro: These structures are rare in everyday speech but appear in formal writing, legal/religious language, literature, and set expressions. Recognizing and occasionally using them signals command of the language's outer edges.

rules.heading: a) Advanced (formal/archaic) subjunctive — the bare base form of the verb (no -s, no "would/should") used after certain verbs/adjectives expressing necessity, demand, or recommendation, especially in formal American English and fixed expressions.
rules.body:
The committee demanded that he resign immediately. (not "resigns")

It is essential that every member be present.

Fixed expressions: So be it. Suffice it to say. Be that as it may. Come what may. God save the Queen.

rules.heading: b) Emphatic "do" in literary contexts — "do/does/did" + bare infinitive used not to form a question or negative, but to add emphasis or formality, common in literary and rhetorical prose.
rules.body:
She did say she would come, but she never showed up. (emphasizing that she really did say it)

Little did I know, this decision did shape the rest of my life.

rules.heading: c) Inverted conditionals with an omitted auxiliary — an extremely formal/literary variant where "if" is dropped, the auxiliary is inverted, and sometimes an entire clause is compressed with ellipsis.
rules.body:
Had I but known, I would have acted differently. ("but" here is an archaic intensifier meaning "only")

Were it not for your generosity, this project would never have existed.

Be it ever so humble, there's no place like home. (archaic subjunctive + inversion, fixed literary expression)

These forms are not required for everyday fluency, but recognizing them is essential for reading literature, historical texts, legal documents, and formal ceremonial language — and using one occasionally in writing adds a deliberate note of gravity or formality.

examples: The judge ruled that the defendant be released on bail.
It is imperative that the report be submitted by Friday.
Be that as it may, the decision has already been made.
Suffice it to say, the meeting did not go well.
She did warn us, but nobody listened.
Little did we know, the storm did far more damage than expected.
Had I but known the risks, I would never have agreed.
Were it not for her intervention, the deal would have collapsed entirely.
Come what may, the team will finish what it started.
The board recommended that the policy be reviewed annually.

commonMistakes.wrong: The committee demanded that he resigns immediately.
commonMistakes.right: The committee demanded that he resign immediately.
commonMistakes.why: The formal subjunctive after "demand that" uses the bare base form, not the third-person -s form.

commonMistakes.wrong: It is essential that every member is present.
commonMistakes.right: It is essential that every member be present.
commonMistakes.why: After "it is essential/imperative/vital that," use the subjunctive "be," not "is."

commonMistakes.wrong: She did said she would come.
commonMistakes.right: She did say she would come.
commonMistakes.why: Emphatic "do/did" is followed by the bare infinitive, not the past tense form — the tense is carried by "did."

commonMistakes.wrong: Had I but know, I would have acted differently.
commonMistakes.right: Had I but known, I would have acted differently.
commonMistakes.why: This inverted structure needs the past participle after "had," matching normal past perfect formation.

commonMistakes.wrong: Were not it for her help, we would have failed.
commonMistakes.right: Were it not for her help, we would have failed.
commonMistakes.why: Word order in this fixed inversion is "Were it not for," not "Were not it for."

exercises.title: Gap-fill
exercises.instructions: Gap-fill (use the correct subjunctive, emphatic "do," or inverted conditional form)

items.prompt: It is essential that everyone ___ (be) informed before the vote.
items.explanation: After “it is essential that,” the formal subjunctive uses the bare base form “be,” not “is.”

items.prompt: The board insisted that the CEO ___ (step) down.
items.explanation: “Insist that” + subjunctive uses the bare base form, with no -s even after “the CEO.”

items.prompt: She ___ (do/warn) us, but we didn't take it seriously.
items.explanation: Emphatic “did” + bare infinitive stresses that the warning genuinely happened.

items.prompt: ___ (had/I/know) the truth sooner, I would have acted differently.
items.explanation: Inverted conditional: “if” is dropped and “had” moves before the subject.

items.prompt: ___ (be/it) not for his quick thinking, the situation would have been far worse.
items.explanation: “Were it not for” is the fixed inverted-conditional opening for this structure.

items.prompt: It is vital that the evidence ___ (be) reviewed carefully.
items.explanation: After “it is vital that,” the subjunctive uses the bare base form “be.”
“Suffice it to say” is a fixed archaic expression, not a literal question form.

items.prompt: He ___ (do/try) to warn them, though few believed him at the time.
items.explanation: Emphatic “did” + bare infinitive stresses that the attempt genuinely happened.

exercises.title: Rewrite / Transformation
exercises.instructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each sentence using the literary/formal structure indicated)

items.prompt: It's necessary that the manager approves the request. (correct to formal subjunctive)
answer: It's necessary that the manager approve the request.
items.explanation: The formal subjunctive after “it's necessary that” uses the bare base form “approve,” not “approves.”

items.prompt: She really did tell them the truth, even if no one believed her. (keep the emphatic "did," rewrite cleanly)
answer: She did tell them the truth, even if no one believed her.
items.explanation: Emphatic “did” + bare infinitive (“did tell”) keeps the stress on the fact that it really happened.

items.prompt: If I had known that earlier, I would have changed my plans. (rewrite using "Had I but known...")
answer: Had I but known that earlier, I would have changed my plans.
items.explanation: “Had I but known” fronts the inverted conditional, with “but” as an archaic intensifier meaning “only.”

items.prompt: If it weren't for your support, this company wouldn't exist. (rewrite using "Were it not for...")
answer: Were it not for your support, this company wouldn't exist.
items.explanation: “Were it not for” is the fixed formal opening replacing “if it weren't for.”

items.prompt: The court ordered that the company pays a fine. (correct to formal subjunctive)
answer: The court ordered that the company pay a fine.
items.explanation: The formal subjunctive after “ordered that” uses the bare base form “pay,” not “pays.”

items.incorrect: It is essential that the report is finalized today.
answer: It is essential that the report be finalized today.
items.explanation: After “it is essential that,” use the subjunctive “be,” not “is.”

items.incorrect: The judge demanded that the witness tells the truth.
answer: The judge demanded that the witness tell the truth.
items.explanation: The formal subjunctive after “demand that” uses the bare base form, not the third-person -s form.

items.incorrect: She did said she would help us.
answer: She did say she would help us.
items.explanation: Emphatic “do/did” is followed by the bare infinitive, not the past tense form — the tense is carried by “did.”

items.incorrect: Had I but know, I would have warned you.
answer: Had I but known, I would have warned you.
items.explanation: This inverted structure needs the past participle after “had,” matching normal past perfect formation.

items.incorrect: Were not it for his generosity, the charity would have closed.
answer: Were it not for his generosity, the charity would have closed.
items.explanation: Word order in this fixed inversion is “Were it not for,” not “Were not it for.”

items.incorrect: Suffice to it say, the results were disappointing.
answer: Suffice it to say, the results were disappointing.
items.explanation: The fixed expression is “Suffice it to say,” not “Suffice to it say.”

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using the formal subjunctive after "It is essential/vital/imperative that..."
items.modelAnswer: It is imperative that the entire team be present for tomorrow's briefing.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using emphatic "do/did" for literary emphasis.
items.modelAnswer: He did try to stop them, though his warning came far too late.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using "Had I but known..." about a past regret.
items.modelAnswer: Had I but known how demanding the course would be, I might have thought twice before enrolling.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using "Were it not for..." to describe something or someone that made a difference in your life.
items.modelAnswer: Were it not for my grandmother's encouragement, I never would have pursued music.

summary: a) Advanced (formal/archaic) subjunctive — the bare base form of the verb (no -s, no "would/should") used after certain verbs/adjectives expressing necessity, demand, or recommendation, especially in formal American English and fixed expressions.
b) Emphatic "do" in literary contexts — "do/does/did" + bare infinitive used not to form a question or negative, but to add emphasis or formality, common in literary and rhetorical prose.
c) Inverted conditionals with an omitted auxiliary — an extremely formal/literary variant where "if" is dropped, the auxiliary is inverted, and sometimes an entire clause is compressed with ellipsis.
